# Spirit baptism — at conversion, after it, or in the sacraments

Every heading and paragraph below is a docstring in those files; every formula is rendered from the encoding they check. If the page and the source disagree, the page is the one that is wrong, and regenerating it is the fix.*

Atoms are numbered propositional variables, numbered once for the whole page, so the same variable means the same claim in every position below. [Reading the logic](../reading-the-logic.md) is the short version of what the notation means. A result marked ⚗ is one this library constructs rather than reports.

## Arguments.SpiritBaptism — baptism in the Spirit: at conversion, after it, or in the sacraments

John promised that the one coming after him would "baptize you with the Holy
Spirit" (Mark 1:8). A reader asks: *is that something every Christian receives
in becoming a Christian, or a second experience to seek after it?* The question
is mostly asked *among* Protestants, and it is about what follows conversion,
not about justification itself. So it is an argument of its own, not a party to
the sola fide dispute.

The views do not line up with the sides of that dispute. Lutherans and Rome
have confessed together "that sinners are justified by faith in the saving
action of God in Christ" (the *Joint Declaration*, §25), and that the Lutheran
teaching it states "does not fall under the condemnations from the Council of
Trent" (§41); Baptists, Pentecostals and the holiness churches did not sign it.
Lutherans, the Reformed, Baptists, Pentecostals and the holiness churches all
hold that faith *alone* justifies; Rome, which holds the sacramental view, does
not hold that faith alone justifies, in the sense Trent condemned. On Spirit
baptism, Lutherans stand partly with Rome (the Spirit is given in water
baptism), and Baptists with the Reformed.

### Three answers, four positions

- **At conversion** — Dunn, the most-cited scholarly case, and Stott. "In one
  Spirit we were all baptized into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13): the baptism
  in the Spirit Christ gives is part of becoming a Christian, so there is no
  second one to seek.
- **After conversion** — two traditions, which this page calls *the
  subsequence views* when it means both.
  - *The Pentecostal view* (the Assemblies of God, 2010; Menzies; Stronstad): at
    conversion the Spirit baptizes into the body of Christ — 12:13 is baptism
    *by* the Spirit, "the Holy Spirit is the instrument" — and in "a subsequent
    and distinct experience, Christ will baptize in the Holy Spirit", as in
    Samaria (Acts 8) and at Ephesus (Acts 19), for empowerment.
  - *The holiness view*: *entire sanctification* — a second work of grace after
    conversion, in which the believer is cleansed from sin and made perfect in
    love — is the baptism with the Spirit. The Church of the Nazarene confesses
    it: entire sanctification "is wrought by the baptism with or infilling of
    the Holy Spirit" (*Manual* 2023, Article X). It is contested from within:
    Wesley, whose teaching on the second work the holiness churches carry on,
    held the second work and declined the name — "they all 'received the Holy
    Ghost' when they were justified" — and in 2010 the faculty of the Nazarene
    seminary, keeping entire sanctification, wrote that they no longer hold that
    reading of the Spirit's baptism exegetically tenable.
- **In baptism and confirmation** — Rome: the Spirit is given in water baptism,
  "new birth in the Holy Spirit", and in confirmation "the full outpouring of the
  Holy Spirit as once granted to the apostles on the day of Pentecost".
  Lutherans hold the first half, and have no sacrament of confirmation. This is
  a later gift too, but a sacramental one: not a second baptism beyond the
  sacraments. The Catholic charismatic renewal, which speaks of a "baptism in
  the Spirit" of its own, is not encoded here.

What is not encoded yet:

- **Tongues.** The Assemblies of God hold that speaking in tongues is the
  *initial evidence* of Spirit baptism — the first outward sign that a believer
  has received it (their paper, summary statement 5). To rate that claim
  honestly needs a reader who grants the subsequence view and still denies the
  evidence doctrine, since everyone who denies subsequence denies it trivially.
  Pentecostal dissenters are known (Fee; Bosworth), but their words could not
  be verified, so the claim is left out rather than rated on memory.
- **Paul's word and Luke's.** "Baptized in the Spirit" may not mean the same in
  1 Corinthians 12:13 as in Acts. Menzies grants that Paul's baptism in the
  Spirit comes at conversion and holds that Luke's is a different, later gift.
  If he is right, the conversion view and the Pentecostal view are partly
  answering different questions. The encoding uses one word for both; a dilemma
  over the word is the natural next step.

### Where it turns

On the Acts narratives. The Pentecostal view holds that they are a pattern for
believers today, and Stott reads them as unrepeatable transitions, "not a
pattern"; read for what they mean, the two exclude each other, so the
Pentecostal view cannot read Acts as transitions at all
(`pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions`), and Stott's reading denies one
of its premises (`stott_undermines_the_pattern`). Read as a pattern, the
narratives meet the variety of Acts itself — the Spirit falls on Cornelius's
household as they hear (10:44), and is promised with baptism at Pentecost
(2:38) — at a step the Assemblies of God contest. So the Pentecostal view must
read Acts as a pattern and answer its variety. What that costs the conversion view is
not checked here: Stott owes an account of why Luke's narratives set no order
for later believers; Dunn avoids the question by denying that the Samaritans
were yet believers before they received the Spirit; and Rome reads Acts 8:17
and 19:6 as confirmation (Catechism 1288).

Weighed as a dispute, nothing is forced (`spirit_baptism_forces_nothing`). The
conversion and sacramental views can be held together, and the two subsequence
views can be held together; every view can be defended, in one of the two
camps, and neither camp is forced.

<a id="onTheConversionStep"></a>
**`onTheConversionStep`**

**The step from 1 Corinthians 12:13 to Spirit baptism at conversion is rated
`disputed`, conservatively.** Dunn and Stott hold it. The Assemblies of God
reject its conclusion, but by denying a ground — that the verse speaks of Christ
baptizing in the Spirit: "'by' is the best translation, indicating that the Holy
Spirit is the instrument" — so they do not contest the step itself. No reader
was sought who grants both grounds and denies the conclusion, so the step is not
rated above the bottom.

```

<a id="actsToSubsequence"></a>
**`actsToSubsequence`**

**The step from the Acts narratives to a second Spirit baptism is well
supported**: grant that believers in Samaria and Ephesus received the Spirit
later, that Luke's Spirit baptism is empowerment, and that his narratives are a
pattern, and the conclusion follows. Unlike the steps rated conservatively here,
this one was audited for a reader who grants all three grounds and denies the
conclusion, and none was found: the readers who reject it deny a ground — Dunn,
that the Samaritans were yet Christians; Stott and Fee, that the narratives are
a pattern. The other steps were not audited in their encoded form, so they stay
at the bottom.

    tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,

```

<a id="wesleyAgainstTheHolinessName"></a>
**`wesleyAgainstTheHolinessName`**

**The holiness step is contested, from within the Wesleyan tradition.** The
Church of the Nazarene holds it (*Manual* 2023, Article X). Wesley grants the
"second change, whereby they shall be saved from all sin and perfected in love", and
denies that it is Spirit baptism: "If they like to call this 'receiving the Holy
Ghost,' they may: only the phrase in that sense is not scriptural and not quite
proper; for they all 'received the Holy Ghost' when they were justified" (to
Joseph Benson, 28 December 1770). The Nazarene seminary faculty, keeping entire
sanctification, "no longer view the American holiness hermeneutic of the
'baptism of the Spirit' as exegetically tenable" (2010).

```lean
def wesleyAgainstTheHolinessName : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work Bib.wesleyLetters
        (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "to Joseph Benson, 28 December 1770"),
    supporting := [Reference.work Bib.nazareneWhitePaper],
    tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="onTheRite"></a>
**`onTheRite`**

**The sacramental step is rated `disputed`, conservatively.** Rome holds it
(Catechism 1302). Westminster rejects the sacramental view, but by denying a
ground — that the Spirit is given in the rite as Rome says: baptism's efficacy
"is not tied to that moment of time wherein it is administered" (XXVIII.6) — so
it does not contest the step itself. No reader was sought who grants the
grounds and denies the conclusion, so the step is not rated above the bottom.

**`onTheSacramentalExclusion`**

**The step from the Spirit given in the sacraments to "no second baptism to

## Arguments.SpiritBaptism.Positions — the four views, and what Acts can carry

Four views, each from a source that holds it — at conversion, Pentecostal,
holiness, sacramental — and two arguments about the Acts narratives: that Acts
gives the Spirit in more than one order, and that its episodes are transitions,
as Stott reads them. Read for what its claims mean, the Pentecostal view must
take the narratives as a pattern: "pattern" and Stott's "not a pattern" exclude
each other (`pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions`). Each is a line of
reason: its own grounds, one step, what it delivers — and, where it answers a
rival, the step it answers with.

#### The conversion view

<a id="corinthiansToConversion"></a>
**`corinthiansToConversion`**

From 1 Corinthians 12:13, read as Christ baptizing in the Spirit, to Spirit
baptism at conversion. Rated `disputed`, conservatively: the Assemblies of God
deny its conclusion by denying a ground, the conversion reading.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{1} \land P_{5}) \rightarrow P_{13}
\]
</div>

<a id="conversionExcludesASecond"></a>
**`conversionExcludesASecond`**

If every believer is baptized in the Spirit at conversion, there is no second
Spirit baptism to seek. Rated `disputed`: Menzies grants that Paul's baptism in
the Spirit comes at conversion and holds that Luke's is a second gift, to be
sought. Whether he denies this step or uses the word in two senses is not yet
encoded.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
P_{13} \rightarrow \lnot P_{14}
\]
</div>

<a id="conversionCase"></a>
**`conversionCase`** — At conversion (Dunn, Stott)

**The conversion view**, as Dunn and Stott hold it: every believer is baptized
in the Spirit at conversion, so there is no second Spirit baptism to seek.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{1} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{5} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; (P_{1} \land P_{5}) \rightarrow P_{13} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{13} \rightarrow \lnot P_{14} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: 1 Corinthians 12:13 — in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.

#### The Pentecostal view

<a id="instrumentalReadingExcludesConversion"></a>
**`instrumentalReadingExcludesConversion`**

The Pentecostal reading of 1 Corinthians 12:13 excludes the conversion
reading: if the Spirit is the instrument baptizing into the body, the verse is
not Christ baptizing in the Spirit. Rated `disputed`, conservatively: Dunn and
Stott deny its conclusion by denying a ground, the instrumental reading.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{1} \land P_{6}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{5}
\]
</div>

<a id="actsToSecond"></a>
**`actsToSecond`**

From the Acts narratives, read as a pattern of empowerment, to a second Spirit
baptism to be sought. Rated `wellSupported`: its rejecters deny a ground, not
the step.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{2} \land P_{7} \land P_{8}) \rightarrow P_{14}
\]
</div>

<a id="pentecostalCase"></a>
**`pentecostalCase`** — After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)

**The Pentecostal view**, as the Assemblies of God hold it: at conversion the
Spirit baptizes into the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13); in a subsequent
and distinct experience Christ baptizes in the Spirit, as in Samaria and at
Ephesus, for empowerment.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{1} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{6} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{2} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{7} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; P_{8} \\
\text{(6)} \quad &amp; (P_{1} \land P_{6}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{5} \\
\text{(7)} \quad &amp; (P_{2} \land P_{7} \land P_{8}) \rightarrow P_{14} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: 1 Corinthians 12:13 — in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.

<a id="secondWorkIsTheBaptism"></a>
**`secondWorkIsTheBaptism`**

The holiness step: the second work of grace is the baptism with the Spirit,
to be sought after conversion. Rated `disputed`: Wesley grants the second work
and denies that it is "receiving the Holy Ghost".

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
P_{10} \rightarrow P_{14}
\]
</div>

<a id="holinessCase"></a>
**`holinessCase`** — A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)

**The holiness view**, as the Church of the Nazarene confesses it: entire
sanctification is a second work of grace, and it "is wrought by the baptism with
or infilling of the Holy Spirit" (*Manual* 2023, Article X). Contested from
within its own tradition, by Wesley and by the Nazarene seminary faculty.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{10} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{10} \rightarrow P_{14} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

#### The sacramental view

<a id="actsTwoToTheSacraments"></a>
**`actsTwoToTheSacraments`**

From Acts 2:38, with the Spirit given in water baptism and fully in
confirmation, to the Spirit given in the sacraments, not in an experience to be
sought. Rated `disputed`, conservatively: Westminster, which holds that the grace
of baptism is not tied to the moment of the rite, denies a ground, not the
step.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{4} \land P_{11} \land P_{12}) \rightarrow P_{15}
\]
</div>

<a id="sacramentsExcludeASeeking"></a>
**`sacramentsExcludeASeeking`**

If the Spirit is given in the sacraments, there is no second Spirit baptism to
seek beyond them. Rated `disputed`, conservatively: the Catholic charismatic
renewal is its natural contester, not yet cited.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
P_{15} \rightarrow \lnot P_{14}
\]
</div>

<a id="sacramentalCase"></a>
**`sacramentalCase`** — In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)

**The sacramental view**, as Rome holds it: the Spirit is given in water
baptism — "new birth in the Holy Spirit" — and fully in confirmation, "as once
granted to the apostles on the day of Pentecost". A later gift, then, but a
sacramental one, not a second baptism beyond the sacraments. Lutherans hold the
first half, and have no sacrament of confirmation, so the view as encoded is
Rome's.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{4} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{11} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{12} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; (P_{4} \land P_{11} \land P_{12}) \rightarrow P_{15} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; P_{15} \rightarrow \lnot P_{14} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{15}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Acts 2:38 — repent and be baptized, and you will receive the gift of the Spirit.

#### What Acts can carry: two readings of the narratives

<a id="varietyExcludesAPattern"></a>
**`varietyExcludesAPattern`**

Acts gives no one order: the Spirit falls as Cornelius's household hears
(10:44), is promised with baptism (2:38), and comes later with the laying on of
hands (8:17; 19:6). So no episode is the pattern. Rated `disputed`: the
Assemblies of God grant Acts 10 and read it as evidence for subsequence.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{3} \land P_{4}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{8}
\]
</div>

<a id="varietyCase"></a>
**`varietyCase`** — Acts gives the Spirit in more than one order

**The variety of Acts**, as an argument: Acts gives the Spirit in more than
one order, so no one episode is a pattern for believers today.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{3} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{4} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; (P_{3} \land P_{4}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{8} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; \lnot P_{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Acts 10:44–48 — the Spirit falls on Cornelius's household before baptism, Acts 2:38 — repent and be baptized, and you will receive the gift of the Spirit.

<a id="transitionsSetNoNorm"></a>
**`transitionsSetNoNorm`**

If the Samaritan and Ephesian episodes are unrepeatable transitions, they set
no norm: no second Spirit baptism is to be sought on their strength. Stott's
step, rated `disputed` conservatively.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
(P_{2} \land P_{9}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{14}
\]
</div>

<a id="transitionCase"></a>
**`transitionCase`** — Acts 8 and 19 as transitions (Stott)

**Acts read as transitions**, as Stott reads it: the later reception of the
Spirit in Samaria and at Ephesus marks steps in the gospel's spread, and sets
no norm.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{2} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{9} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; (P_{2} \land P_{9}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{14} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; \lnot P_{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="narrativesReadAsPattern"></a>
**`narrativesReadAsPattern`**

Reading the narratives as a pattern: the Assemblies of God and Stronstad.

```lean
def narrativesReadAsPattern : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work Bib.stronstadCharismaticTheology,
    supporting := [Reference.work Bib.agBaptismPositionPaper],
    tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="asAPattern"></a>
**`asAPattern`**

The Acts narratives, **read as a pattern for believers today**.

```lean
def asAPattern : Reading Claim :=
  { name := "as a pattern for believers today",
    commits := p Claim.actsNarrativesAreNormative,
    source := narrativesReadAsPattern }
```

<a id="pentecostalOnAPattern"></a>
**`pentecostalOnAPattern`** — After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad), read as a pattern for believers today

The Pentecostal view, with the Acts narratives read as a pattern.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{1} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{6} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{2} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{7} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; P_{8} \\
\text{(6)} \quad &amp; (P_{1} \land P_{6}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{5} \\
\text{(7)} \quad &amp; (P_{2} \land P_{7} \land P_{8}) \rightarrow P_{14} \\
\text{(8)} \quad &amp; P_{2} \rightarrow P_{8} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: 1 Corinthians 12:13 — in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.

#### Readings, written down

<a id="conversionReading"></a>
**`conversionReading`**

The conversion view's world: every believer baptized in the Spirit at
conversion, 1 Corinthians 12:13 read as Christ baptizing in the Spirit, the
episodes of Acts as transitions, no pattern, and no second baptism to seek.

```lean
def conversionReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.cor12_13IsBaptismByTheSpirit => False
    | Claim.actsNarrativesAreNormative => False
    | Claim.secondSpiritBaptismToBeSought => False
    | Claim.entireSanctificationIsSecondWork => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="pentecostalReading"></a>
**`pentecostalReading`**

The Pentecostal view's world: 1 Corinthians 12:13 as baptism by the Spirit
into the body, Luke's Spirit baptism as empowerment, the narratives a pattern,
and a second baptism to seek.

```lean
def pentecostalReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.cor12_13IsChristBaptizingInTheSpirit =>
      False
    | Claim.spiritBaptismAtConversion => False
    | Claim.actsEpisodesAreTransitions => False
    | Claim.spiritGivenInTheSacraments => False
    | x => True
```

#### What Acts can carry

<a id="pentecostalOnAPattern_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`pentecostalOnAPattern_is_satisfiable`**

**The first reading is coherent**: the Pentecostal view with the narratives as a
pattern contradicts nothing by itself.

```lean
theorem pentecostalOnAPattern_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    pentecostalOnAPattern.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="whereTheVarietyMeetsThePattern"></a>
**`whereTheVarietyMeetsThePattern`**

**Why the variety of Acts stands against reading it as a pattern.** The crux is
the step from Acts 10 and 2:38: the Spirit comes as they hear, is promised with
baptism, and comes later with hands laid on, so no one episode is the pattern.
What it breaks is the Pentecostal view's premise that the narratives are a
pattern. The step is disputed: the Assemblies of God grant Acts 10 and read it
as evidence for subsequence.

**Why *Acts gives the Spirit in more than one order* stands against *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad), read as a pattern for believers today*.**

- **The crux:** \\((P_{3} \land P_{4}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{8}\\), a premise of *Acts gives the Spirit in more than one order*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(P_{3}\\), \\(P_{4}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(P_{8}\\) cannot be held together with \\((P_{3} \land P_{4}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{8}\\) and \\(P_{3}\\), \\(P_{4}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(P_{3}\\) Acts 10:44–48 — the Spirit falls on Cornelius's household before baptism — *consensus*: Acts 10:44-48
  - \\(P_{4}\\) Acts 2:38 — repent and be baptized, and you will receive the gift of the Spirit — *consensus*: Acts 2:38
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [`assemblies-of-god-baptism-holy-spirit-2010`](../bibliography.md#assemblies-of-god-baptism-holy-spirit-2010)

## Arguments.SpiritBaptism.Dispute — the four views weighed

The four views as parties to one dispute: at conversion; after it, as the
Pentecostals hold; after it, as the holiness tradition holds; and in baptism and
confirmation, as Rome holds. The Pentecostal and holiness views are *the
subsequence views*: both hold a second baptism in the Spirit, after conversion,
to be sought. Who defeats whom is computed from their premises and checked by the
kernel.

### How to read the verdicts

- **Defeats.** One position contradicts another — denies one of its premises,
  its conclusion, or a claim it derives on the way — and is not the weaker of
  the two. A defeat that runs both ways is a *standoff*.
- **Weakest link.** A position is only as strong as its least-supported premise
  or step. Every party here rests on something rated `disputed`, the lowest
  rating, so no rating breaks a standoff.
- **Forced.** Accepted however every standoff is resolved.
- **Can be defended.** Held by some consistent position that answers every
  attack on its members, itself or through an ally.
- **Not forced.** Some consistent position leaves it out — which is not the same
  as false.

### What the solver computed

Four standoffs, and nothing else. The conversion view stands off against both
subsequence views, and so does the sacramental view; the two subsequence views
do not attack each other, and neither do the conversion and sacramental views.
Nothing is forced (`spirit_baptism_forces_nothing`). Every view can be defended
(`conversion_defensible`, `pentecostal_defensible`, `holiness_defensible`,
`sacramental_defensible`), in one of two camps, and nothing joins them: the
conversion and sacramental views together, and the Pentecostal and holiness
views together.

That is where the question stands in the literature, and the page says so rather
than choosing. The conversion and sacramental views agree that there is no
second baptism in the Spirit to seek, and differ over the rite, which this
dispute does not weigh. What would decide between the two camps is argued, not
weighed: what Luke's narratives are (`pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions`
says the Pentecostal view must read them as a pattern), and whether
Paul's word at 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Luke's are the same baptism — a question
not yet encoded.

#### The dispute

<a id="viewNode"></a>
**`viewNode`**

The package each view argues from.

```lean
def viewNode : View → ArgumentPackage Claim :=
  fun x =>
    match x with
    | View.conversion =>
      conversionCase
    | View.pentecostal =>
      pentecostalCase
    | View.holiness =>
      holinessCase
    | View.sacramental =>
      sacramentalCase
```

<a id="spiritBaptismDispute"></a>
**`spiritBaptismDispute`**

The dispute over Spirit baptism: every view can be held without
contradiction, delivers its conclusion, and has its steps rated.

```lean
def spiritBaptismDispute : Dispute Claim View :=
  { node := viewNode,
    consistent := spiritBaptismDispute._proof_1,
    sound := spiritBaptismDispute._proof_2,
    rated := spiritBaptismDispute._proof_7 }
```

<a id="conversion_stands_with_the_sacraments"></a>
**`conversion_stands_with_the_sacraments`**

**The conversion and sacramental views can be held together**: one reading
satisfies both — every believer baptized in the Spirit at conversion, the Spirit
given in the sacraments, and no second baptism to seek.

What this does not claim: that the two agree. They differ over what the rite
does, which this dispute does not weigh; the result says only that nothing
encoded here makes them contradict each other.

```lean
theorem conversion_stands_with_the_sacraments :
    spiritBaptismDispute.StandTogether [View.conversion, View.sacramental]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="the_subsequence_views_stand_together"></a>
**`the_subsequence_views_stand_together`**

**The two subsequence views can be held together**: a second baptism to
seek, whether read as empowerment or as the second work of grace. Whether it is
the same second experience, the encoding does not say.

```lean
theorem the_subsequence_views_stand_together :
    spiritBaptismDispute.StandTogether [View.pentecostal, View.holiness]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="viewDefeats"></a>
**`viewDefeats`**

The defeats of the dispute, as a table.

```lean
def viewDefeats : View → View → Prop :=
  fun x x_1 =>
    match x, x_1 with
    | View.conversion,
      View.pentecostal => True
    | View.conversion,
      View.holiness => True
    | View.pentecostal,
      View.conversion => True
    | View.pentecostal,
      View.sacramental => True
    | View.holiness,
      View.conversion => True
    | View.holiness,
      View.sacramental => True
    | View.sacramental,
      View.pentecostal => True
    | View.sacramental,
      View.holiness => True
    | x, x_2 => False
```

<a id="instDecidableRelViewViewDefeats"></a>
**`instDecidableRelViewViewDefeats`**

The table is finite, so membership in it is decidable.

```lean
def instDecidableRelViewViewDefeats : DecidableRel viewDefeats
```

Each view's weakest link: `disputed` for every one.

def viewStrength : View → ℕ :=

Each view's weakest link, as its package computes it.

<a id="spiritBaptismDispute_defeats"></a>
**`spiritBaptismDispute_defeats`**

**Who defeats whom**, all 16 pairs: four standoffs, and nothing else. The
conversion view and each subsequence view defeat each other — "no second to
seek" against "a second to seek" — and the Pentecostal view also denies the
conversion reading of 1 Corinthians 12:13. The sacramental view and each
subsequence view defeat each other on the same point. Every cell is computed by
`Horn.defeats?` and checked by the kernel.

```lean
theorem spiritBaptismDispute_defeats : ∀ (i j : View),
    spiritBaptismDispute.defeats i j ↔ viewDefeats i j
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

**`spiritBaptismFinite`**

The dispute in the form the verdict solver computes with.

```lean
def spiritBaptismFinite : Solver.Finite spiritBaptismDispute.defeats :=
  {
    parties :=
      [View.conversion,
        View.pentecostal,
        View.holiness,
        View.sacramental],
    complete := spiritBaptismFinite._proof_1,
    defeats := fun i j => decide (viewDefeats i j),
    spec := spiritBaptismFinite._proof_2 }
```

**Nothing supports anything**, in all 16 pairs. Every cell is computed by

Each view's case is part of its own and of no other's. Every cell is computed

#### What the dispute decides

<a id="spiritBaptismSettlesNothing"></a>
**`spiritBaptismSettlesNothing`**

Why nothing is forced: every view has a defeater. The conversion view has the
Pentecostal, the Pentecostal and holiness views have the conversion view, and the
sacramental view has the Pentecostal.

**Nothing prevails outright: every party is defeated by another.**

- *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)* defeats *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*.
- *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*.
- *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)*.
- *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)* defeats *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 4 defeats and 0 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`spiritBaptismDispute_defeats`](#spiritBaptismDispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*, weakest at *disputed*:

<a id="spirit_baptism_forces_nothing"></a>
**`spirit_baptism_forces_nothing`**

**Nothing is forced.** Every view is in a standoff the dispute cannot resolve,
and every weakest link is `disputed`, so no rating breaks a tie.

What this does not claim: that the question is idle. Each view can be defended;
what the dispute cannot do is choose between readings rated alike.

```lean
theorem spirit_baptism_forces_nothing : Framework.grounded
    spiritBaptismDispute.defeats = ∅
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="conversionStandsWithTheSacraments"></a>

and answers both subsequence views, itself.

- None of *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*, *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:

- A position holding *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*, *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)* can be held, and it holds *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*; *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* conflicts with *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*: *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*, and *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)* defeats *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*.
- None of *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*, *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:
  - *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)* defeats *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*, and *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*.
  - *A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)* defeats *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)*, and *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)*.
  - *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)* defeats *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)*, and *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *After conversion (Assemblies of God; Menzies, Stronstad)*.
  - *A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)* defeats *In baptism and confirmation (Catholic)*, and *At conversion (Dunn, Stott)* defeats *A second work of grace (the holiness tradition)*.

<a id="pentecostal_not_forced"></a>
**`pentecostal_not_forced`**

**Nor is it forced.** A maximal defensible position holds the conversion and
sacramental views, and cannot hold the Pentecostal view with them. What would
decide is argued, not weighed: what the Acts narratives are
(`pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions`).

```lean
theorem pentecostal_not_forced : ¬Framework.SkepticallyAccepted
    spiritBaptismDispute.defeats View.pentecostal
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

#### What the Pentecostal view can read Acts as

<a id="pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions"></a>
**`pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions`**

**The Pentecostal view cannot read Acts as transitions.** Its own premise is
that Luke's narratives are a pattern for believers today, and Stott's reading
says, in its own words, that they are "not a pattern"
(`Testimony.Meanings.SpiritBaptism.joins`). So what the view holds, read for
what its claims mean, denies the transitions reading outright.

What this claims: the Pentecostal view must read the Acts narratives as a
pattern; the other reading is not open to it. What it does not claim: that the
pattern reading is right. Read as a pattern, the narratives still meet the
variety of Acts (`whereTheVarietyMeetsThePattern`), at a step the Assemblies of
God contest.

Before the two readings were joined by meaning, this was a dilemma with two
horns, and the transitions horn broke only at Stott's step from transitions to
no norm. Joined, the horn is not there to break: no reader can hold the
Pentecostal view and read Acts as transitions.

```lean
theorem pentecostal_cannot_read_acts_as_transitions : Entails
    pentecostalCase.held (notP Claim.actsEpisodesAreTransitions)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="stott_undermines_the_pattern"></a>
**`stott_undermines_the_pattern`**

**Stott's reading meets the Pentecostal view at its premise.** Read for what
its claims mean, Acts as transitions denies that the narratives are a pattern,
and that is one of the Pentecostal view's premises. Before the join it met the
view only at Stott's step, as a reason not to seek a second baptism; now it
contradicts what the view rests on. Whether that attack is a defeat is a
question of ratings, and this argument's dispute does not seat Stott's reading
as a party.

```lean
theorem stott_undermines_the_pattern : UnderminesOn transitionCase
    pentecostalCase (p Claim.actsNarrativesAreNormative)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```
